questions.q: What did Lesson 12's 'before' numbers show that the old cluster-wide average had hidden?
options: That all three AZs were underutilized
That eastus2-2 was running at ~96% peak utilization while the cluster-wide average blended to ~72% and looked fine
That the warehouse data was corrupted
That the application had a memory leak
questions.explain: The precise per-AZ numbers confirmed exactly what the average had masked: one zone running far hotter than the reported aggregate suggested.

questions.q: What did Lesson 14's 'after' numbers (roughly 46-48% across all three zones) actually prove?
options: That the fix made no measurable difference
That the topologySpreadConstraints fix corrected the distribution problem — all three zones now land within a tight band under the same real sale traffic
That the sale traffic had decreased
That a fourth availability zone was added
questions.explain: A tight band across all three zones under the same real load is direct evidence the distribution problem was solved, not just a hopeful assumption.

questions.q: What is the actual compromise Theo proposes to Casey and Dana?
options: Permanently triple all replica counts
Raising the sale-window ceiling from 12 to 16 replicas based on the real post-fix baseline, paired with a permanent per-AZ spread guarantee and the existing off-hours minimum kept in place
Remove the autoscaler and run fixed capacity year-round
Let Casey and Dana each manage a separate half of the cluster
questions.explain: The proposal raises the ceiling with real data for the specific window it's needed, keeps the per-AZ guarantee permanently, and avoids paying for that ceiling around the clock.

questions.q: Why does the per-AZ guarantee (maxSkew: 1) still matter even after the ceiling is raised?
options: It doesn't matter anymore once the ceiling is higher
Without it, a bigger ceiling just gives the scheduler more room to repeat the original imbalance at a larger scale
It only affects billing, not scheduling
It was removed as part of this compromise
questions.explain: A higher ceiling without the spread guarantee could reproduce the same AZ-skew problem, just with more total pods involved.

questions.q: Why does this proposal satisfy Dana's concern specifically, beyond just being 'a number everyone agreed to'?
options: Because it is backed by measured data and bounded to the sale window rather than running as permanently pinned capacity, giving her a defensible figure for budget review
Because Dana was outvoted and had no real say
Because the proposal has nothing to do with cost
Because it removes Finance from future capacity decisions entirely
questions.explain: A ceiling grounded in real Inform-phase data and scoped to the window it's needed gives Dana something defensible, rather than a number won by argument alone.
